---
title: Your first publication audit
---

This tutorial uses fictional public content. The extension observes rendered
files and leaves them unchanged; no policy is delivered to the browser.

## 1. Enable the audit and render

From this checkout, run `quarto render` or use your editor's **Render Project**
control. The supplied `_quarto.yml` already enables auditing. For an existing
project, install the extension as described in the repository's `README.md`, then
merge this into project YAML:

```yaml
content-security-protocol:
  enabled: true
```

Security options belong in project/profile configuration, not this QMD's front
matter. Normal rendering should retain the following content and native link.

## 2. Inspect the rendered page

This fictional page exercises ordinary HTML, a [native destination](#details),
and mathematics $x^2 + y^2 = z^2$. The audit observes final bytes and leaves them
unchanged. No policy is delivered to the browser.

::: {#audit-details .callout-note collapse="true"}
## A small interactive state

Inline script/style hashes are candidates for review, not automatic permission.
:::

Open and close this native callout. The ordinary audit inventories its final
files; that alone does not test the expanded state. The README's optional
interaction-profile example uses this stable QMD ID for a separately requested
browser check. Your normal preview needs no author JavaScript or helper script.

## 3. Read the private report {#details}

After rendering, run the installed command from your project directory:

```sh
quarto run _extensions/kai-prince-sfhea/content-security-protocol/cli.ts report
```

That is the GitHub installation path. For a local checkout installation, omit
`kai-prince-sfhea/`. The new `report` command currently requires the unpublished
local candidate. It returns verified Markdown with file/page counts, findings
and coverage; it writes no new file and refuses stale state. The audit stays
private under `.quarto`, outside the website's resources.

## 4. Edit and render again

Change this QMD's title. Calling `report` before rerendering should refuse stale
source state. Render again, then repeat `report` to read the new current audit.
Historical reports remain available, but a saved report cannot certify later
output. Keep any manually saved copy outside your published project.

## 5. Optionally prepare a host-header candidate

After the ordinary audit works, use one explicit installed command to prepare
private report-only header text:

```sh
quarto run _extensions/kai-prince-sfhea/content-security-protocol/cli.ts headers
```

That keeps the existing Netlify default. For Cloudflare Pages static hosting:

```sh
quarto run _extensions/kai-prince-sfhea/content-security-protocol/cli.ts headers --adapter cloudflare-pages
```

For a local installation, omit `kai-prince-sfhea/` as above. Open the resulting
private `headers-netlify.txt` or `headers-cloudflare-pages.txt` under
`.quarto/content-security-protocol`. Read the declared policy and findings
before any separate host setup. The Cloudflare file uses one uniform static
rule; its complete header line has a strict host limit. Unsupported host
configuration is refused. Neither command installs `_headers`, changes this
page, blocks scripts, sends reports or deploys your site.

Keep report-only first. Enforcement requires the README's separate review
workflow and actual host-response checks. Successful rendering and private
candidate preparation do not establish hosted enforcement or security.

## Next steps

Open `README.md` in the repository for the options reference, which introduces
policy choices after the ordinary audit works. Its hosting and accessibility guide covers
optional trusted-page execution and separately reviewed header delivery.
Automated findings are evidence for review, not a security or WCAG certificate.
